_about: Settings the extractor (book/scripts/build-writing-data.js) applies on top of the book's Key Terms. Edit here, then run: node book/scripts/build-writing-data.js
_mode: 'ask' (default): the helper only asks questions about this concept. 'may-demonstrate': the helper may show a short example on another topic, then ask the student to make the same move.
_alwaysInFocus: Concepts in every focus, whatever chapter the prompt comes from: the Chapter 1-2 core every argumentative essay needs. The structure terms (family 'writing') are always in focus too.
_provisional: Stand-ins for the writing chapter's structure terms, so the app can be built and tested before that chapter exists. Wording is a placeholder, not the book's. Replace each with the chapter's own Key Terms when it is drafted.

provisional.title: Thesis
provisional.definition: The main conclusion an essay argues for, stated early and plainly enough that a reader can find it.

provisional.title: Topic sentence
provisional.definition: A sentence, usually at the start of a paragraph, that says what the paragraph contributes to the argument.

provisional.title: Paragraph unity
provisional.definition: Each paragraph does one job in the argument, such as giving one reason, supporting it, or answering one objection.

provisional.title: Evidence
provisional.definition: Facts, examples, data, or testimony offered to show that a reason is true.

provisional.title: Objection and reply
provisional.definition: Stating the strongest reason against your conclusion and answering it.

provisional.title: Signposting
provisional.definition: Words that tell the reader how a sentence or paragraph relates to the argument, such as indicator words and transitions.

provisional.title: Clear example
provisional.definition: A specific case that shows what a general claim means or why it is true.

provisional.title: Sentence variety
provisional.definition: Varying the length and structure of sentences so that the emphasis falls where the argument needs it.

_provisionalPrompts: Stand-in prompts for the writing chapter. Replace with the chapter's own Writing Prompts when it is drafted.

provisionalPrompts.text: Write a short argumentative essay (400–700 words) on a question you care about. State your thesis in the first paragraph, give each main reason its own paragraph with a topic sentence and evidence, and answer the strongest objection.

Choose a claim from a recent campus email, opinion piece, or policy, and write a short essay arguing for or against it. Give a clear thesis, two or three reasons, and a paragraph that states and answers an objection.
Revise one of your earlier writing assignments for this course into an argumentative essay with a thesis, topic sentences, and an objection and reply.
